display_title: US Regulators Sue Dollar General Over Alleged Overcharging
display_title_he: רשויות הפיקוח בארה"ב תובעות את דולר ג'נרל בגין גביית יתר
short_summary: The FTC and 20 states have filed a federal lawsuit against Dollar General, accusing the discount chain of systematically charging higher prices at checkout registers than advertised on store shelves.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers

sources.name: CNBC
sources.title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers

paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), alongside attorneys general from twenty U.S. states, has initiated a major lawsuit against Dollar General, the largest discount retail chain in the United States. Filed in federal court in Nashville, Tennessee, the 95-page legal complaint accuses the company of engaging in systemic pricing misconduct across its vast network of more than 20,000 stores. Regulators assert that the retail giant has repeatedly overcharged consumers by ringing up higher prices at cash registers than those displayed on store shelves. Officials contend that this practice effectively extracts millions of dollars from vulnerable shoppers who rely heavily on discount outlets to stretch their household budgets amidst high food and fuel costs.

The joint federal and state legal action stems directly from evidence accumulated through undercover operations and prior investigative reporting. In late 2025, a media investigation revealed that Dollar General had failed over 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections across twenty-three states over a three-year period. Following those public disclosures, FTC investigators conducted secret shopper tests in multiple states, including Ohio, Pennsylvania, Missouri, and Maryland, over a two-and-a-half-month span beginning in January. According to court filings, every single undercover visit uncovered multiple instances of overcharging. At one Cleveland store, nearly fourteen percent of purchased items registered higher prices at the checkout than advertised on the shelves.

Authorities allege that the retailer's internal policies designed to ensure accurate pricing exist primarily on paper while achieving very little in practice. Although company procedures instruct employees to replace outdated shelf tags on designated days, workers reported being consistently unable to complete these duties due to chronic understaffing. In some instances, overwhelmed employees admitted to discarding updated price labels to avoid disciplinary measures from store supervisors. Furthermore, regulators highlighted that Dollar General lacked tracking mechanisms to verify whether replacement tags were actually affixed to shelves, leaving store-level price discrepancies unaddressed.

Dollar General strongly disputed the allegations, maintaining that its overarching goal remains total pricing alignment between shelves and registers. Responding to the complaint, the company argued that minor pricing discrepancies occur naturally in retail environments and emphasized that store staff are fully empowered to correct errors for customers. Executives expressed surprise at the lawsuit, noting that the firm had produced over 200,000 documents and more than 350 gigabytes of data during discussions. Nevertheless, market reactions were swift, with company shares dropping approximately four percent following the public announcement.

This federal legal action reflects heightened enforcement against deceptive pricing practices across the retail sector. Shortly before the FTC filing, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced a $1.875 million settlement with Dollar General to resolve persistent overcharging complaints within the state. As low-income households cope with sustained economic pressure from elevated living expenses, public officials from diverse political backgrounds are increasingly eager to demonstrate active measures safeguarding consumer paychecks.

facts.fact: The Federal Trade Commission and 20 US states sued Dollar General in federal court in Nashville over alleged widespread customer overcharging.
Dollar General operates over 20,000 stores across the United States.
A Guardian investigation in December 2025 found Dollar General failed over 4,300 government price inspections in 23 states over three years.

FTC undercover shoppers made test purchases in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Missouri, and Maryland, finding overcharges on every single visit, including a Cleveland store where nearly 14% of items were overcharged.
Dollar General employees reported that understaffing prevented them from changing price tags on time, with some throwing away tags to avoid trouble.
Dollar General stated its goal is 100% price accuracy, defended its practices, and noted it provided over 200,000 documents and 350 gigabytes of data to investigators.
Dollar General shares dropped about 4% following the announcement of the lawsuit.
New York Attorney General Letitia James previously settled overcharging allegations with Dollar General for $1.875 million.
